🌇 Good Wednesday afternoon. Today's newsletter, edited by Alex Fitzpatrick, is 586 words, a 2-min. read. Thanks to Carolyn DiPaolo for copy editing.

 
 
1 big thing — Axios interview: Private Trump-Thune AI chat
 
Senate Majority Leader John Thune talks to reporters this month on Capitol Hill. Photo: Tierney L. Cross for The New York Times

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) says that President Trump is "not really dug in" against government guardrails for AI, despite Trump's public campaign against new restrictions on the technology, Axios' Stef W. Kight reports from an interview today.

Thune tells Axios that he spoke privately with Trump as the AI issue was getting "pretty hot" a few weeks ago, and believes that some of Trump's strong pushback lately is against public "paranoia and noise around the subject."

  • Thune reads Trump's position as a preference for companies coming up with ways to secure their systems, rather than Congress or the administration, and relying more on experts to provide guidance on how to address threats.

👂 Zoom out: Thune has Trump's skepticism in one ear and tech leader alarm in the other.

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called Thune to discuss AI safety before issuing his latest public warning on the tech's risks, Thune tells Axios.

Thune says: "I do think that the threats are real. I think you have to take them seriously."

  • "But I do also think that there are people who are ... doing a lot of fearmongering."

👀 What to watch: Thune's AI bill, which has not yet been reintroduced this Congress, puts the onus on tech companies to mitigate AI risks — but also calls for some federal oversight.

  • It requires AI companies to report on any serious risks with frontier models and to come up with plans to address the concerns.

2. 🛰️ Prepare for space war
 
Illustration: Maura Losch/Axios

Three U.S. military leaders in just as many days changed how the public talks about war in space, including the secretive weapons already among the stars, Axios' Colin Demarest reports.

  • Last week, and in quick succession:
  1. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said America has "on-orbit space control weapons" — a historic acknowledgment.
  2. Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess told reporters that "it was time" to have such a discussion and be clear-eyed about Russian and Chinese capabilities, including "being able to grapple a satellite and move it to a different orbit."
  3. Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine said troops must be "prepared to fight, endure and win in global, contested environments, from the seabed to cislunar space."

The big picture: Space fights will happen. They'll look nothing like conflict on the ground or at sea. And the consequences will be enormous.

The outlook for data center power demand
 
 

As AI models scale, their massive computational needs are putting unprecedented pressure on power grids.

Goldman Sachs Research projects AI will drive an increase of 170% in global data center power demand by 2030, adding the equivalent of Japan's entire electricity consumption.

4. 📚 1 fun thing: Romi, the library robot
 
Photo: Gitanjali Poonia/Axios

The country's first library robot helper lives at Arizona's Mesa Gateway Library, Axios Mesa's Gitanjali Poonia reports.

  • Romi is part tour guide, part selfie station — and easily the library's most futuristic helper.

👋🏻 Romi can greet visitors in eight languages and lead them to different sections of the building.

  • Visitors can touch the screen on its belly to look up books.

How AI debt is reshaping global credit markets
 
 

Companies are increasingly turning to bond markets and relying less on internal cash to fund the AI buildout.

The impact: this shift is driving a wave of AI-related debt as companies draw upon a mix of markets to finance the multi-year investment cycle.
